[MUQATIL:20:9-12/r2] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | At the valley Tuwa, God calls Moses and orders him to remove sandals made from the skin of an unritually dead donkey; Tuwa is the valley’s name and means the purified valley.
[YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p253#2/r7] YAHYA-SALLAM, d. 200 · author | holds | When Moses reached it, he reached what he had thought was fire.
[YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p254/r1] YAHYA-SALLAM, d. 200 · قتادة | reports | Qatāda says Moses' two sandals were made from the hide of a dead donkey; Moses removed them and approached.
[FARRA:v2p175/r3] FARRA, d. 207 · author | holds | With the call addressed to Moses, إني أنا ربك begins with kasra; the readings also allow the call to encompass أني and موسى.
[TAB-FULL:v16p22/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · وهب بن منبه | reports | As Moses approached, the fire withdrew; when he turned back it came closer, and he felt afraid.
[ZAJJAJ:v3p350#2/r5] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | reports | With fatḥa on أني, the sense is ‘he was called by the words that I am your Lord,’ and أني is accusative.
[ZAJJAJ:v3p350#2/r6] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | reports | With kasra on إني, the call is ‘O Moses, I am your Lord.’
[NAHHAS:v3p33/r5] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | نودي means “he was told,” which explains the variant readings of يا موسى أني.
[NAHHAS:v3p33/r6] NAHHAS, d. 338 · الحسن وأبو جعفر وأبو عمرو | reports | They read أني with fatḥa, meaning “he was called that I am”; أن is accusative.
[NAHHAS:v3p33/r7] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | reports | Readers who give the hamza kasra understand Moses as saying “I am.”
[SULAMI:v1p436#3/r1] SULAMI, d. 412 · جعفر | reports | Moses recognized God's call as it enveloped every hair from every direction; awe and majesty confirmed it, and the divine self-identification left him stunned and annihilated. God alone bears and answers His address; Moses is its intermediary locus.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v3p395/r1] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | holds | The thing Moses came to was the fire, which was light.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v3p395/r2] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | One view is that God addressed Moses directly and alone.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v3p395/r3] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | Another view says God made the light speak with a call from His inseparable light, calming Moses so he could bear God's command.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v14p365#2/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas says Moses approached the fire, saw it in a jujube tree, and marveled at the bright fire amid intense green: the fire did not spoil the tree and its water did not dim the fire; then he heard a call from the tree.
[JISHUMI:v6p4638/r1] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | prefers | On the preceding question about divine istiwāʾ, the author says the sounder view of Abū ʿAlī is that it means power; the Kullābī account of an act or attribute called istiwāʾ is unintelligible.
[JISHUMI:v6p4638/r3] JISHUMI, d. 494 · أبو جعفر وابن كثير وأبو عمرو | reports | They read “annī” with fatḥa, understood as “because I am your Lord”; the others use kasra as the beginning of a new quotation, “he said: I am.”
[JISHUMI:v6p4638/r4] JISHUMI, d. 494 · أبو جعفر ونافع وابن كثير وأبو عمرو | reports | These readers open the final yāʾ in “innī”; the remaining readers leave it quiescent.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p56#2/r1] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · أبو عمرو وابن كثير | reports | Abu ʿAmr and Ibn Kathir read أني with fatḥ, meaning Moses was called with the words that I am your Lord; the others read kasr, meaning he was called, O Moses, or treating the call as speech.
[TABRISI:20:9-12/r10] TABRISI, d. 548 · وهب | reports | Wahb reports that Moses heard a call from the tree, answered that he heard a voice but could not see its place, and learned by the response and a miracle that the caller was his Lord.
[TABRISI:20:9-12/r9] TABRISI, d. 548 · ابن عباس | reports | As Moses approached, the fire appeared in a jujube tree; its brilliant light and vivid green amazed him before the tree called him.
[TABRISI:20:9-16/r1] TABRISI, d. 548 · أبو جعفر وابن كثير وأبو عمرو | reports | These readers open the initial alif in anī anā rabbuka; the remaining readers pronounce it with kasra.
[TABRISI:20:9-16/r6] TABRISI, d. 548 · أبو علي | holds | The kasra treats the speech as direct quotation after Moses is called; the fatḥa connects it to what he was called with, since calling may take a preposition.
[TABRISI:20:9-16/r7] TABRISI, d. 548 · أبو علي | holds | For passive nūdiya, a clause cannot serve as the passive subject; an implicit pronoun must do so, or Moses can be the subject because he was already mentioned.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p273/r1] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | The feminine pronoun refers to the fire; when Moses came to it, he was called.
[RAZI-FULL:v22p14/r12] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbas describes a green tree glowing white from bottom to top like fire, with neither the flame changing its greenness nor the tree’s moisture dimming the flame; Moses saw great light and heard angels glorifying God.
[RAZI-FULL:v22p14/r13] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · وهب | reports | Wahb narrates that Moses approached the apparent fire with dry sticks; it moved toward him, retreated, repeatedly tempted him, then vanished, while the branch glowed skyward and a dazzling light appeared.
[RAZI-FULL:v22p14/r16] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The immediate-sequence particle faʾ does not exclude a brief interval between Moses’ arrival and the call.
[QURTUBI-FULL:20:11-12/r2] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Qabas is a flame from fire, and miqbās is likewise a firebrand or fire-taking implement.
[QURTUBI-FULL:20:11-12/r3] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Qabistu and iqtibās can refer to taking fire; iqtibās can also mean acquiring knowledge.
[QURTUBI-FULL:20:11-12/r4] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · اليزيدي | reports | Al-Yazīdī distinguishes aqbastu someone knowledge from qabastu him fire; aqbastu is used when seeking knowledge for someone.
[QURTUBI-FULL:20:11-12/r5] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · الكسائي | reports | Al-Kisāʾī permits aqbastuhu for either fire or knowledge; qabastuhu also applies to both.
[QURTUBI-FULL:20:11-12/r6] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Hudā here means hādiyan, a guide.
[QURTUBI-FULL:20:11-12/r7] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The pronoun in أتاها refers to the fire.
[QURTUBI-FULL:20:11-12/r8] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Moses was called from the tree's direction and vicinity, as in Sūrat al-Qaṣaṣ.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:20:11-12/r1] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | When Moses reached the fire, he found a white flame burning in a green tree and was called by name.
[NASAFI-FULL:v3p51#4/r1] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Moses found white fire blazing through a green tree, either a jujube or an osage tree.
[NASAFI-FULL:v3p51#4/r2] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | reports | He found no one by the fire; a report says it moved away when he approached and neared him when he stopped seeking it.
[NASAFI-FULL:v3p51#4/r3] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Moses was called.
[QASHANI:20:6-12/r6] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | When Moses connects with the fire, he is called beyond fiery curtains of majesty; “I am your Lord” is God's manifestation veiled in a fiery form.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p315/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الجمهور | reports | The majority read innī with kasra, supplying a speech verb or treating the call as speech; Ibn Kathīr and Abū ʿAmr read wa-annī with fatḥa.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p315/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Moses knew the speaker through divinely created knowledge or a miracle; Muʿtazilites require miraculous proof and reject necessary knowledge as incompatible with accountability.
[SAMIN-DURR:20:11/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | prefers | The implied subject of the passive verb نودي is Moses.
[SAMIN-DURR:20:11/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | rejects | An alternative takes the implied subject to be the verbal noun, meaning 'the call was called'; the author calls this weak.
[SAMIN-DURR:20:11/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | rejects | The clause يا موسى cannot be the passive verb's subject because a clause cannot serve as a subject.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p276#2/r1] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | Moses came to the fire and drew near to it, whereupon he was called by name.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p276#2/r2] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | The call to Moses is compared with the account of his being called from the right side of the valley, in the blessed spot, from the tree. | mentions 28:30
[BIQAI-FULL:v5p13/r4] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The passive 'he was called' first conceals the caller and then magnifies the summons when Moses is named.
[BURSEVI:v5p284#2/r1] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās says Moses saw a green tree encircled from base to top by brilliantly burning white fire, with no person nearby; neither the fire dimmed the tree nor the tree's water dimmed the fire.
[BURSEVI:v5p284#2/r2] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | reports | Moses heard the angels glorifying God, saw a light too intense for eyes, covered his eyes, and was overcome with fear and astonishment before calm was sent upon him.
[BURSEVI:v5p284#2/r3] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · قالوا | reports | The tree is identified variously as a green samura, an ʿawsaja, a blackberry-like thorn tree, or a jujube; these trees contain no fire unlike other trees.
[BURSEVI:v5p284#2/r4] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · قالوا | reports | One four-part classification says worldly fire eats but does not drink, green-tree fire drinks but does not eat, Hellfire both eats and drinks, and Moses' fire neither eats nor drinks.
[BURSEVI:v5p284#2/r5] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · قالوا | reports | A second classification distinguishes fire with burning but no light (Hell), light without burning (Moses), both (worldly fire), and neither (trees).
[BURSEVI:v5p284#2/r6] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | In the inward reading, light signifies love and fire signifies ardent love; when Moses' love and

longing were full, the essential light appeared in the form of attribute-fire, burned away his selfhood, and brought single-hearted orientation.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p166#2/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · ابن عباس | reports | In a report from Ibn ʿAbbās, the fire was in a verdant, luxuriant jujube tree.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p166#2/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · عبد الله بن مسعود | reports | ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd says the fire was in a samura tree.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p166#2/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · بعضهم | reports | Another reported location is an awsj tree.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p166#2/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · وهب بن منية | reports | Wahb ibn Munabbih narrates that Moses saw a huge fire in a very green al-ʿalīq tree: it grew without burning the tree, repeatedly approached and withdrew as he tried to take a flame, then became a brilliant pillar reaching skyward. Moses feared and wondered at it; the extraordinary scene culminated in angelic praise and calm. No grading is stated.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p167/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · قالوا | reports | One fourfold scheme says worldly fire eats but does not drink, green-tree fire drinks but does not eat, Hellfire does both, and Moses’s fire does neither.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p167/r10] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Al-Ālūsī classifies the pre-prophetic marvel as irhāṣ, a precursor miracle that the Muʿtazilites reject.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p167/r11] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | prefers | The apparent passive-subject pronoun refers to Moses.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p167/r12] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · بعضهم | reports | Another grammatical proposal takes the passive subject as a verbal noun: the calling occurred.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p167/r13] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · بعضهم | reports | A third proposal makes the quoted words يا موسى the subject by treating the call as including speech and taking that wording as the intended message.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p167/r14] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الكوفيون | reports | The Kūfans treat calling as equivalent to saying; the Basrans instead posit an omitted saying verb, so the meaning is that Moses was called and told يا موسى.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p167/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · قالوا | reports | A second scheme classifies fires by light and burning: worldly fire has both, tree fire neither, Hellfire burns without light, and Moses’s fire shines without burning.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p167/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · ابن عباس | reports | Another view, reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, is that this was not fire but light from God’s light; the verse calls it fire because that is how Moses perceived it.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p167/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · أبو حيان | prefers | Abū Ḥayyān favors interpreting the phenomenon as light rather than actual fire; al-Māwardī also adopts this view.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p167/r5] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · سعيد بن جبير | reports | Saʿīd ibn Jubayr says it was fire itself and one of God’s veils.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p167/r6] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · النبي | reports | Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī transmits the Prophet’s statement that God’s veil is fire and that uncovering it would burn every creature reached by the radiance of His face; al-Baghawī cites it and al-Khāzin says Muslim recorded it.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p167/r7] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · بعض المعتزلة | rejects | Some Muʿtazilites use the verse’s apparent immediate call to reject reports that an interval passed between Moses’s arrival and the call.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p167/r8] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | rejects | Al-Ālūsī replies that an interval of the reported kind does not undermine those accounts.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p167/r9] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · بعض المعتزلة | rejects | Some Muʿtazilites deny that a miracle could appear when Moses reached the fire before his prophetic commission, unless it were a miracle for another prophet.
[TABATABAI:20:11-14/r2] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Moses knew with certainty that his Lord spoke to him: in revelation the addressee apprehends no other speaker, consistent with the Quran's account of divine communication. | mentions 42:51
[TABATABAI:20:11-14/r3] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | A prophet's first reception of prophecy or mission is immediate and certain; needing rational proof would make it acquired inference rather than reception from the unseen.
[TABATABAI:20:11-14/r4] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Other passages place a veil or intermediary in Moses' call; this is compatible with revelation, since the message is experienced as God's when attention passes over the unseen mediator. | mentions 19:52, 28:30, 20:13
[TABATABAI:20:13-14/r1] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | The passive 'he was called' omits the agent with a subtle effect and hints that the sign appeared to Moses suddenly.
[ASAD-NOTES:20:11#n8/r1] ASAD-NOTES, d. 1412 · author | holds | Asad notes that the passive wording literally means “he was called.”
[SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p783/r3] SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT · author | holds | Taha uses atyan more than fifteen times and maji four; Naml uses maji eight times and atyan thirteen, fitting their respective verb choices here. | mentions 20:11, 27:8
[STUDYQURAN:20:11/r1] STUDYQURAN · Q, Ṭ | reports | It is said that God called to Moses from a tree in the valley.
[STUDYQURAN:20:11/r3] STUDYQURAN · JJ | reports | One interpretation takes the referent to be the tree from which God called Moses.
[STUDYQURAN:20:11/r4] STUDYQURAN · IK, R, Ṭ, Bg, R | reports | Another interpretation identifies it with the fire Moses saw, which consumed the tree. | mentions 20:10

<<end of notes>>
